concepts.name: Resources and URIs
concepts.summary: Explain that a REST API models things as resources, each identified by a URI such as /users/42.

concepts.name: Collections and single items
concepts.summary: Recognise the pattern of a plural collection URI (/orders) and an item URI (/orders/17) beneath it.

concepts.name: HTTP methods as actions
concepts.summary: Describe how GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE express reading, creating, replacing, updating and removing resources.

concepts.name: Status code classes
concepts.summary: Remember that 2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and recall common codes like 200, 201, 404 and 500.

concepts.name: JSON representations
concepts.summary: Understand that a resource is exchanged as a representation, typically JSON, separate from the server's internal storage.

concepts.name: Statelessness
concepts.summary: Explain that each request carries all information needed to process it, so the server keeps no client session between calls.

misconceptions.text: REST is the same thing as HTTP or JSON, so any API that uses them is RESTful.
URIs should contain verbs like /getUser or /deleteOrder to say what they do.
A response is successful whenever the server replies, so 200 is fine for everything.

concepts.name: Resource naming conventions
concepts.summary: Apply consistent naming: plural lowercase nouns, hyphenated words, no verbs, and no file extensions.

concepts.name: Nested resources and relationships
concepts.summary: Model relationships with paths like /customers/5/orders and judge when to keep nesting shallow.

concepts.name: Safe and idempotent methods
concepts.summary: Distinguish safe methods from idempotent ones and say which of GET, PUT, DELETE and POST has which property.

concepts.name: Choosing correct status codes
concepts.summary: Pick codes such as 201 with Location, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409 to match what actually happened.

concepts.name: Query parameters for filtering
concepts.summary: Use query parameters to filter, sort and select fields on a collection rather than creating new endpoints.

concepts.name: Basic pagination
concepts.summary: Return large collections in pages using limit/offset or page parameters along with total or next-page information.

concepts.name: Consistent error response body
concepts.summary: Return errors in a uniform JSON structure with a code, message and details alongside the proper status code.

misconceptions.text: POST and PUT are interchangeable for creating resources.
Deeper URI nesting always gives a clearer API, so /a/1/b/2/c/3/d/4 is good design.
Using 200 with an error message in the body is acceptable, so the status code need not reflect failure.

concepts.name: PUT versus PATCH semantics
concepts.summary: Analyse when full replacement (PUT) or partial update (PATCH, merge patch or JSON Patch) fits an update and its effect on idempotency.

concepts.name: Cursor-based pagination
concepts.summary: Compare offset and cursor pagination in terms of consistency under inserts, performance and navigation, and design cursor responses.

concepts.name: API versioning strategies
concepts.summary: Contrast URI, header and media-type versioning and decide which changes are breaking versus backward compatible.

concepts.name: Problem Details error format
concepts.summary: Structure errors using the standard problem details fields (type, title, status, detail, instance) with field-level validation errors.

concepts.name: Authentication and authorization design
concepts.summary: Design API access with bearer tokens or API keys, and separate 401 authentication failures from 403 permission failures.

concepts.name: Idempotency keys for POST
concepts.summary: Analyse how retries cause duplicate creations and use an idempotency key so POST can be retried safely.

concepts.name: HTTP caching with validators
concepts.summary: Use Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match/If-Match to enable caching and prevent lost updates.

concepts.name: Modelling non-CRUD actions
concepts.summary: Analyse options such as sub-resources or state fields for operations like cancel or publish that do not map neatly to CRUD.

misconceptions.text: PATCH is just another name for PUT and behaves identically.
Versioning is only needed when you remove a field; adding fields or changing meaning never breaks clients.
401 and 403 mean the same thing and either can be used for any access failure.

concepts.name: Hypermedia and HATEOAS trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate the Richardson maturity model and when hypermedia links justify their cost for discoverability and decoupling.

concepts.name: Evolution without breaking clients
concepts.summary: Judge change strategies such as additive changes, tolerant readers, Sunset and Deprecation headers, and migration timelines.

concepts.name: Rate limiting and quotas
concepts.summary: Analyse rate limiting schemes and communicate limits through 429, Retry-After and rate limit headers.

concepts.name: Long-running operations
concepts.summary: Design asynchronous operations using 202, a status resource and polling or callbacks rather than blocking requests.

concepts.name: Concurrency control
concepts.summary: Apply optimistic concurrency with ETags and 412 or 409 responses to analyse and prevent conflicting writes.

concepts.name: Bulk and batch operations
concepts.summary: Evaluate designs for bulk create or update, including partial-success reporting such as 207 versus all-or-nothing.

concepts.name: Contract-first with OpenAPI
concepts.summary: Evaluate describing an API in an OpenAPI document to drive documentation, validation, mocks and contract testing.

concepts.name: Webhooks and event notification
concepts.summary: Analyse webhook design including signed payloads, retries, ordering and delivery guarantees.

misconceptions.text: An API is truly RESTful as soon as it uses resource URIs and HTTP methods, even without hypermedia.
Bulk endpoints should always be atomic, since partial success is confusing and wrong.
A generated OpenAPI document is documentation enough and needs no design review or contract testing.

concepts.name: API style selection
concepts.summary: Evaluate when REST, GraphQL, gRPC or event-driven interfaces best fit given clients, performance, coupling and team constraints.

concepts.name: API governance and style guides
concepts.summary: Create organisation-wide design guidelines and automated linting that keep many teams' APIs consistent.

concepts.name: Designing for the client experience
concepts.summary: Create APIs whose naming, defaults, errors, SDKs and documentation minimise time to first successful call.

concepts.name: Resource granularity and aggregation
concepts.summary: Evaluate coarse versus fine-grained resources, embedding and expansion, and aggregation layers to balance round trips and coupling.

concepts.name: Long-term API lifecycle management
concepts.summary: Create lifecycle plans covering design review, versioning policy, deprecation, telemetry-driven change and retirement.

concepts.name: Security threat modelling for APIs
concepts.summary: Evaluate an API design against threats such as broken object-level authorisation, mass assignment and excessive data exposure.

concepts.name: Consistency and scale trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate how eventual consistency, caching layers and replication shape the guarantees an API can honestly promise.

misconceptions.text: REST is always the best choice, and GraphQL or gRPC are merely fashionable replacements.
Strict consistency rules matter less than flexibility, so each team should design its API freely.
Authentication on every endpoint is enough, with no need for per-object authorisation checks.
